title: CHAPTER FIFTEEN. On eternal death
english: These things concerning eternal life: there follows eternal death, which is the separation of the impious from God and all the saints because of impenitence and unbelief, and so their own malice, in which with the Devil they will endure without end the wrath of God, the bite of conscience, and thence ignominy of every kind and anxiety with unspeakable torment.

title: I–II. Names of eternal death; receiving subject the impious
english: I. The nomenclature of eternal death is taken from 2 Thess. 1:8–9, where it is called eternal destruction; also Wis. 4:19; and Heb. 6:2 eternal damnation; from place and reception hell, prison, furnace of fire, place of torments, lake and winepress of wrath, lake of fire, pit, chains of darkness, Gehenna, eternal fire, outer darkness.

II. The receiving subject are the impious who do not have true and heavenly wisdom, nor the wedding garment of Christ's righteousness through faith, not obeying the Gospel, but worshiping the beast — the fearful, unbelieving, fornicators, idolaters, and the like.

title: III. Reason of eternal death: absence of the highest good and presence of evil
english: III. The reason of eternal death is both the absence of the highest good and the presence of evil. Absence of good is separation from God, the principal evil of the damned — they are deprived of God's face and fruition entirely. From separation from God arises separation from the saints; denial of all compassion. Present external evils: a horrible place, society of the Devil. Internal: (1) God's wrath; (2) the bite of conscience (the gnawing worm); (3) ignominy, anguish, envy, fear, horror, and perpetual despair.

title: IV–V. Efficient/deficient cause; end; canons 1–2 on place and God's concurrence
english: IV. The efficient — or rather deficient — proximate and adequate cause is the impenitent unbelief of the impious with malice.
V. The end intended by God is the glory of his patience and justice; the terminus of that death is none — it will be continued forever.

Canons: (1) That the damned have a certain place and will be tormented with eternal fire is plain from Scripture; the constitution of hell and what sort the fire is is not revealed — be not curious. (2) Although God is not the procreating cause of damnation but the damned themselves, he yet concurs as just judge by preparing, threatening, inflicting, and continuing punishments.

title: Canons 3–5: degrees of punishment; against extinction and finite torment
english: (3) Just as in eternal life there will be degrees of glory in the elect, so in the damned there will be degrees of punishments from deserts. Equality in the defect of God's vision and in eternity; distinction of degrees from deserts.
(4) That eternal death is nothing other than eternal extinction of soul and body is a harmful and most absurd Socinian opinion.

(5) That the hour of torments will at last have some end — Origenists and some Anabaptists dream, but in vain: eternal death and life are opposed in the same sense; the worm does not die; the smoke ascends forever and ever.

title: Canons 6–8: pious taste hell's pains tempered; impious carry hell daily; broad way
english: (6) The pious in this life sometimes also feel some of hell's torments, which yet God's grace so tempers that they make them seek him more ardently. Christ felt the pains of hell in our place.
(7) The impious, although they carry their hell about with them daily in this life, yet most rarely feel it because of incredible stupor, and under it at last they sink.
(8) The way which most pursue is the way of hell, which the more it is loved the more it ought to be suspect to the pious.

title: Canon 9: meditation on hell; Liber II corona — consensus of confessions — Cap. 15 / Liber II close
english: (9) Perpetual meditation on hell ought to rouse us from the flesh's security and license to sin; in persecutions to comfort by confidence of eternal immunity. Let us descend into hell while living lest we descend while dying (Bernard). It serves repentance and consolation.

For the rest: as concerning Sacred Scripture in Book I, so concerning man's highest good and its opposite evil in Book II — among theologians against papist tyranny who embrace the Augsburg, Helvetic, French, English, and Belgian confessions, by God's benefit there is consensus. For which the God of peace is to be prayed that he further confirm it. Closing distich of Bernard of Morlaix: No one can speak or write or meditate the joys of the just nor the torments of the wicked.
